meta.title: Contextual chronology
meta.description: Events that fill the gaps between the entries in the report's own chronology (Appendix B). Appendix B records major crimes and massacres; these entries record the legal, political and institutional steps between them — the mandates, laws, plans, rulings and admissions that make the pattern legible. They are marked as context so the report's chronology remains distinguishable.

items.event: The Hussein–McMahon correspondence opens
items.note: Ten letters between Sharif Hussein of Mecca and the British High Commissioner in Egypt, Sir Henry McMahon, running to March 1916, in which Britain undertook to support Arab independence in return for a revolt against the Ottomans. Whether Palestine was inside or outside the promised area has been disputed ever since; Britain's own 1939 committee of inquiry could not agree, and the correspondence was made to sit alongside two later commitments that contradicted it.

items.event: The Sykes–Picot Agreement divides the Ottoman Arab provinces
items.note: A secret Anglo-French understanding, concluded with Russian assent, allotting spheres of control and placing most of Palestine under an undefined international administration. It was signed while the Hussein–McMahon undertakings were still live, and was published by the Bolsheviks in November 1917, days after the Balfour Declaration.

items.event: Faisal–Weizmann Agreement signed, conditional on Arab independence
items.note: Faisal's handwritten reservation made the agreement void if Arab independence was not granted. It was not, and the agreement lapsed; it is nonetheless still cited as Arab consent.

items.event: Article 22 of the League Covenant creates the mandate system
items.note: The Covenant described mandated peoples as communities whose existence as independent nations could be provisionally recognised, and the mandatory as holding a sacred trust of civilisation until they could stand alone. Palestine was classed as a Class A mandate, the category nearest to independence — the legal premise against which the Mandate's administration is measured.

items.event: King–Crane Commission reports that the Zionist programme could be carried out only by force of arms
items.note: The American commission appointed by the Paris Peace Conference found that the non-Jewish population, then about 90% of Palestine, was emphatically against the programme, and that its realisation would require a military occupation. The report was suppressed until 1922.

items.event: Nebi Musa riots in Jerusalem
items.note: The first mass communal violence of the Mandate period. The Palin Commission of Inquiry attributed Arab fears to the Balfour Declaration and to the belief that self-determination had been denied. Its report was never published.

items.event: San Remo conference assigns Britain the Mandate for Palestine, incorporating the Balfour Declaration
items.note: A commitment made by one people to a second people over the land of a third was converted into an instrument of international law.

items.event: The Histadrut is founded, with Hebrew labour as policy
items.note: The General Federation of Jewish Labour organised the Yishuv's economy around the exclusive employment of Jewish workers and the exclusive purchase of Jewish produce. It was a labour policy in form and a separation policy in effect, and the campaigns it ran against Arab labour on Jewish-owned land are documented in its own records.

items.event: Jaffa riots; the Haycraft Commission finds the cause is Arab fear of dispossession
items.note: 47 Jews and 48 Arabs killed. The commission concluded that Arab hostility was not religious but arose from political and economic causes connected with Jewish immigration.

items.event: Churchill White Paper affirms the Jewish national home while denying an intention to displace the Arab population
items.note: The first British attempt to reconcile two commitments that were not reconcilable on the ground.

items.event: League of Nations approves the Mandate for Palestine
items.note: Article 2 obliged Britain to secure the establishment of the Jewish national home; the Arab majority is referred to only as the 'non-Jewish communities', and only its civil and religious — not political — rights are protected.

items.event: Jabotinsky publishes 'The Iron Wall'
items.note: Argues that Zionist colonisation can proceed only behind an iron wall of force that the native population cannot break, because no people ever consents to its own displacement. Cited in the report as an accurate description of what followed.

items.event: Jabotinsky publishes 'The Iron Wall'
items.note: Ze'ev Jabotinsky sets out the programme in terms: 'Zionist colonisation must either stop, or else proceed regardless of the native population. Which means that it can proceed and develop only under the protection of a power that is independent of the native population - behind an iron wall, which the native population cannot breach.' The clearest statement of the settler-colonial analysis of the project is a Zionist one, which is why Rebuttal 23 turns on it.

items.event: The Palestinian Citizenship Order comes into force
items.note: The Order created a Palestinian citizenship for the inhabitants of the Mandate, held by Arabs and Jews alike. It governed until 14 May 1948 and was repealed by Israel's Nationality Law of 1952, which replaced it with a status the refugees of 1948 could not meet the conditions for.

items.event: Brit Shalom founded in Jerusalem, arguing for a binational state
items.note: Founded at Arthur Ruppin's home after the 14th Zionist Congress; members included Martin Buber, Gershom Scholem, Hugo Bergmann, Hans Kohn and Henrietta Szold. It held that Palestine belonged to both peoples and that both were entitled to self-determination. Part of the Jewish dissent from political Zionism treated in §10 of the report; it disintegrated by mid-1936.

items.event: Shaw Commission reports on the 1929 riots
items.note: Found the fundamental cause to be Arab landlessness and unemployment arising from Jewish land purchase and immigration.

items.event: Hope Simpson report and the Passfield White Paper
items.note: Found that the cultivable land available could not support further large-scale settlement without displacing Arab cultivators. The White Paper's restrictions were reversed by the MacDonald Letter of February 1931 after Zionist political pressure in London.

items.event: Irgun founded, splitting from the Haganah
items.note: The paramilitary organisation later designated a terrorist organisation by the British authorities; its commander from 1943 was Menachem Begin, later Prime Minister.

items.event: Haavara (Transfer) Agreement signed with Nazi Germany
items.note: Enabled the emigration of German Jews to Palestine with part of their assets, and brought German goods into Palestine during the international boycott of Nazi Germany. Documented in the German Foreign Ministry archives; treated in §1.2A of the report.

items.event: Izz ad-Din al-Qassam killed by British police near Ya'bad
items.note: His death precipitated the general strike and the Arab Revolt of 1936–39.

items.event: Arab general strike begins; the Arab Revolt opens
items.note: The longest general strike in colonial history to that point, demanding an end to Jewish immigration and land transfers and the establishment of representative government.

items.event: Peel Commission recommends partition and the 'transfer' of the Arab population
items.note: The first official proposal for the compulsory removal of some 225,000 Arabs from the proposed Jewish state. The word transfer enters the official record here.

items.event: Ben-Gurion's diary: the compulsory transfer of Arabs 'could give us something we never had'
items.note: The Ben-Gurion Archives at Sde Boker. Reproduced in Appendix C and §1.3 of the report.

items.event: Neturei Karta founded in Jerusalem in rejection of Zionism on religious grounds
items.note: Rabbis Amram Blau and Aharon Katzenelbogen broke from the Jerusalem branch of Agudath Israel over its accommodation with the Zionist institutions of the Yishuv. The doctrinal basis is the Three Oaths of Ketubot 111a. A fringe group then and now, numbering in the hundreds to low thousands, and disowned across the Haredi world, including by Satmar (§23.1).

items.event: Special Night Squads formed under Orde Wingate with Haganah members
items.note: British-trained joint units used in the suppression of the revolt. Moshe Dayan and Yigal Allon served in them; the methods were carried into 1948.

items.event: The Évian Conference declines to admit Jewish refugees
items.note: Delegates of 32 states met at Évian-les-Bains to consider German and Austrian Jewish refugees. With the sole exception of the Dominican Republic, none agreed to raise its admissions. Britain attended on condition that Mandatory Palestine would not be discussed; the United States sent a businessman rather than a senior official and proposed no increase in its quotas. On 13 July the Nazi party newspaper Völkischer Beobachter drew the conclusion: "No one wants them."

items.event: The St James's Palace Conference meets in separate rooms
items.note: Britain convened the Arab and Zionist delegations at St James's Palace to settle Palestine's future; the Arab Higher Committee refused to sit with the Zionist delegation, so Colonial Secretary Malcolm MacDonald held parallel talks and two official photographs were taken. Both sides rejected the British proposals of 15 March, and Britain then imposed its own policy in the White Paper of May 1939.

items.event: British White Paper limits Jewish immigration and land purchase
items.note: Proposed an independent Palestine within ten years with an Arab majority. Rejected by the Zionist leadership; the Irgun and Lehi campaigns against British rule follow.

items.event: The White Paper caps Jewish immigration to Palestine
items.note: Britain limited Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years and provided that further immigration would require the consent of the Arab majority; land transfer regulations the following year restricted Jewish land purchase in all but about 5 per cent of Palestine. The policy was rejected by the Zionist leadership and by the Palestine Arab parties alike. By 1944 only 51,000 of the 75,000 certificates had been used. The cap held through the years of the extermination in Europe.

items.event: Land Transfer Regulations restrict Jewish land purchase to 5% of Palestine
items.note: By 1947, after four decades of purchase, Jewish ownership stood at about 6–7% of the land; the 1947 partition plan nonetheless allotted 55% of the territory to the Jewish state.

items.event: Biltmore Program demands a Jewish Commonwealth in the whole of Palestine
items.note: Adopted in New York; the movement's public abandonment of partition in favour of the whole territory.

items.event: American Council for Judaism constituted in opposition to the establishment of a Jewish state
items.note: Formed by thirty-six Reform rabbis after a meeting at Atlantic City on 1 June 1942 opposing the CCAR resolution supporting a Jewish army in Palestine. It held that Judaism is a religion and not a nationality, and advocated a democratic Palestine with equal political rights irrespective of religion. The position had already been overturned inside the movement by the Columbus Platform of 1937 (§23.2).

items.event: British Defence (Emergency) Regulations enacted
items.note: Administrative detention, house demolition, closure and deportation powers. Denounced at the time by Jewish jurists in Palestine as Nazi-like; retained by Israel after 1948 and still applied in the occupied territory today.

items.event: The Theodor Herzl is intercepted off Palestine
items.note: The Haganah refugee ship reached the coast carrying about 2,600 Jewish passengers, most of them survivors of the Nazi camps, outside the British quota. A banner along the rail read: "The Germans destroyed our families and homes - don't you destroy our hopes." A Royal Navy boarding party took the ship, three passengers were killed resisting, and the passengers were deported to the British internment camps on Cyprus, through which Yad Vashem records 52,000 people passing between 1946 and 1949. The photograph of the banner is authentic and is frequently recaptioned; the interception was carried out by the Mandatory power, not by the population of Palestine.

items.event: UNSCOP reports, and its majority recommends partition
items.note: The UN Special Committee on Palestine divided: a majority proposed partition with economic union, a minority a federal binational state. Neither plan was put to the population it concerned. The majority plan became the basis of Resolution 181 three months later.

items.event: UN General Assembly Resolution 181 recommends partition
items.note: Allotted 55% of the territory to a Jewish state whose population would have been 45% Arab, at a time when Jewish residents were about a third of the population and owned about 7% of the land.

items.event: Plan Dalet adopted
items.note: The Haganah plan providing for the destruction of villages and the expulsion of their populations. Its execution began before the declaration of the state and before any Arab army entered Palestine.

items.event: Deir Yassin attacked by the Irgun and Lehi
items.note: More than a hundred villagers killed, five weeks before the regular armies of the Arab states crossed on 15 May. Roughly 300,000 Palestinians had been displaced by that date, which is the fact the account of a flight ordered by Arab leaders is offered to displace. Rebuttal 20.

items.event: Declaration of the State of Israel
items.note: By this date roughly 300,000 Palestinians had already been displaced. The war with the Arab states began the following day.

items.event: UN General Assembly Resolution 194 affirms the right of return
items.note: Resolved that refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date. Reaffirmed by the General Assembly annually since.

items.event: The armistice agreements draw the Green Line
items.note: Separate agreements with Egypt (24 February), Lebanon (23 March), Jordan (3 April) and Syria (20 July) fixed the ceasefire lines that became the 1967 borders. Each agreement stated in terms that the line was not a political or territorial boundary and was without prejudice to a final settlement.

items.event: Israel admitted to the United Nations
items.note: Resolution 273 recalls Israel's undertakings to implement Resolutions 181 and 194. Neither was implemented.

items.event: Israel signs the Lausanne Protocol, and is admitted to the UN the next day
items.note: The protocol accepted the 1947 partition map as the working basis for talks and the return of refugees as a subject for them. Israel was admitted to the United Nations on 11 May 1949 on an undertaking to implement Resolutions 181 and 194; the Lausanne talks then produced nothing, and neither undertaking was carried out.

items.event: Absentees' Property Law transfers refugee property to the state
items.note: The legal mechanism by which the land and homes of the displaced were expropriated, including from 'present absentees' who remained inside Israel.

items.event: Jordan annexes the West Bank
items.note: The Jordanian parliament formally united the two banks and extended Jordanian nationality to the Palestinians under its control. Only Britain and Pakistan recognised the annexation; the Arab League treated the territory as a trust. The measure was undone in law only in 1988.

items.event: UNRWA begins operations
items.note: Established by General Assembly Resolution 302 (IV) in December 1949, the agency started work with about 750,000 registered refugees. It was created as a temporary body pending a political settlement, and its mandate has been renewed ever since, which is the plainest measure of how little the settlement has advanced.

items.event: Law of Return grants every Jew worldwide the right to immigrate
items.note: Read with the Absentees' Property Law and the 1952 Citizenship Law, it is the pairing that B'Tselem and Amnesty cite as the foundation of the demographic regime.

items.event: The Nationality Law comes into force and repeals Palestinian citizenship
items.note: Passed by the Knesset on 1 April 1952 and in force from 14 July, the law made every Jew an Israeli national on immigration under the Law of Return, while a former Palestinian citizen acquired nationality only by proving registration on 1 March 1952 and continuous presence since the establishment of the state. Refugees who had fled or been expelled could satisfy neither condition, and the law repealed the Palestinian citizenship they had held since 1925.

items.event: Land Acquisition Law retroactively legalises the seizure of Arab land
items.note: Completed the transfer of expropriated property; by the mid-1950s the state and the Jewish National Fund controlled the great majority of the land.

items.event: The Prevention of Infiltration Law criminalises refugee return
items.note: The statute made unauthorised entry by a person who had been in Palestine before 1948 a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment and deportation, and applied to the refugees attempting to return to their own villages. It converted the physical prevention of return into a permanent legal regime.

items.event: Israel invades Sinai in concert with Britain and France
items.note: The Suez war was preceded by the secret Protocol of Sèvres, in which the three governments agreed the Israeli attack would supply the pretext for an Anglo-French intervention. Israel withdrew from Sinai and Gaza in March 1957 under American and Soviet pressure, having held Gaza for four months.

items.event: Military government over Palestinian citizens of Israel
items.note: Eighteen years of permits, curfews, closed areas and administrative detention applied to citizens on the basis of nationality. Abolished in November 1966, five months before the occupation of the West Bank and Gaza began.

items.event: Basic Law: Israel Lands bars the sale of state and JNF land
items.note: The Basic Law prohibits transferring ownership of land held by the state, the Development Authority or the Jewish National Fund — together about 93 per cent of the territory of Israel. Read with the JNF's own constitution, under which its land is held for the Jewish people, it is the instrument that converted the expropriations of 1948–1953 into a permanent tenure regime.

items.event: Childers publishes 'The Other Exodus' in The Spectator
items.note: Erskine Childers examined the BBC and United States monitoring records of every Middle East broadcast of 1948 and reported 'not a single order, or appeal, or suggestion about evacuation from Palestine from any Arab radio station, inside or outside Palestine, in 1948'. He had asked the Israeli Foreign Ministry for the texts in 1958 and was promised them; none was supplied. Rebuttal 20.

items.event: The PLO is founded in Jerusalem
items.note: The first Palestinian National Council convened in East Jerusalem, then under Jordanian rule, and adopted the Palestinian National Charter. The organisation was created under Arab League auspices and was taken over by the guerrilla factions after 1967, with Yasser Arafat elected chairman in 1969.

items.event: Israel's Supreme Court bars the Socialists' List from the Knesset election
items.note: EA 1/65 Yeredor. The Court upheld the exclusion of a list drawn from the banned al-Ard movement, although the Basic Law: The Knesset then contained no provision permitting it, on the reasoning that a purpose denying the state's existence is an unlawful purpose. The first judicial limit on the political rights of Palestinian citizens; Justice Haim Cohn dissented.

items.event: Military rule over Palestinian citizens of Israel is abolished
items.note: For eighteen years the Palestinians who remained inside the 1949 armistice lines and held Israeli citizenship lived under a military government: permits to travel between towns, curfews, administrative detention and closed areas, administered under the Defence (Emergency) Regulations inherited from the Mandate. It ended eight months before the same regulations were applied to the West Bank and Gaza, where they remain in force.

items.event: The Moroccan Quarter of Jerusalem is demolished
items.note: Within days of the city's capture, 135 houses were bulldozed and about 650 residents expelled to clear the plaza in front of the Western Wall. Two mosques and a zawiya were destroyed. The demolition preceded any decision on the status of the territory and set the pattern for the administrative annexation of East Jerusalem that followed on 28 June.

items.event: Allon Plan sets the template for settlement of the occupied territory
items.note: Proposed retaining the Jordan Valley and a chain of settlements; the geography of Area C follows it closely.

items.event: Military Order 101 criminalises assembly, procession and publication
items.note: The order made a gathering of ten or more persons on a political matter a criminal offence without a permit from the military commander, along with printing, displaying or distributing material of political significance. It remains in force, and is the instrument under which Palestinian protest in the West Bank has been prosecuted for more than fifty years.

items.event: The Khartoum summit answers with the three noes
items.note: The Arab League summit resolved on no peace with Israel, no recognition and no negotiations, while also resolving to seek withdrawal by political means. The resolution is cited as proof that no partner existed; the same document's commitment to a political rather than military course is usually left out of the citation.

items.event: Theodor Meron advises the Israeli government that civilian settlement violates the Fourth Geneva Convention
items.note: The Foreign Ministry's own legal counsel, in a memorandum to the Prime Minister's office: 'civilian settlement in the administered territories contravenes the explicit provisions of the Fourth Geneva Convention.' Settlement proceeded regardless. The strongest single admission in the settlement record.

items.event: Kfar Etzion established — the first settlement in the occupied West Bank
items.note: Followed by more than 300 settlements and outposts and, by 2026, over 700,000 settlers.

items.event: UN Security Council Resolution 242 emphasises the inadmissibility of the acquisition of territory by war
items.note: The cornerstone of every subsequent negotiation, and the provision the ICJ relied on in its 2024 advisory opinion.

items.event: Security Council Resolution 252 declares the measures in Jerusalem invalid
items.note: The Council held that all legislative and administrative measures taken by Israel to change the status of Jerusalem, including expropriation of land and property, are invalid and cannot change that status, and called on Israel to rescind them. It was the first of a line of resolutions saying the same thing, none of which was complied with.

items.event: Arson at Al-Aqsa Mosque; the Organisation of the Islamic Conference is founded in response
items.note: The fire, set by an Australian Christian acting alone on a millenarian conviction, destroyed Saladin's 12th-century minbar. UN Security Council Resolution 271 of 15 September 1969 condemned Israel's failure to observe earlier resolutions on Jerusalem; twenty-five states met at Rabat on 25 September and founded the OIC.

items.event: Sharon's clearance operations in the Gaza refugee camps
items.note: Thousands of homes demolished to drive wide roads through the camps for military access; some 16,000 people displaced a second time.

items.event: October War
items.note: Ended the post-1967 assumption that the territorial status quo was costless; it did not alter the status of the occupied territory.

items.event: Gush Emunim is founded to settle the occupied territory
items.note: The movement organised the settlement of the West Bank as a religious obligation, beginning with repeated unauthorised attempts at Sebastia near Nablus. Successive governments treated its faits accomplis as facts to be regularised rather than offences to be removed, and its outposts became the template for the process still running.

items.event: The Rabat summit names the PLO the sole legitimate representative
items.note: The Arab League summit recognised the PLO as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, ending Jordan's claim to negotiate for the West Bank. It is the decision that made the PLO the address for any settlement, and the reason the 1988 Jordanian disengagement followed.

items.event: General Assembly Resolution 3236 affirms the right to self-determination and return
items.note: The Assembly reaffirmed the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination, national independence and sovereignty, and the right of the displaced to return to their homes and property, and granted the PLO observer status. Arafat had addressed the Assembly on 13 November.

items.event: General Assembly Resolution 3379 equates Zionism with racism
items.note: Adopted by 72 votes to 35 with 32 abstentions, and revoked on 16 December 1991 by Resolution 46/86 as the price of Israel's participation in the Madrid conference. The episode is recorded here because both the adoption and the revocation are regularly cited without the other.

items.event: Land Day: six Palestinian citizens of Israel killed protesting land expropriation in the Galilee
items.note: The first general strike by Palestinian citizens of Israel, and the event that marked their emergence as a political community within the state.

items.event: The Koenig Memorandum is leaked
items.note: Written in April 1976 by Yisrael Koenig, the Interior Ministry's district commissioner for the north, the memorandum proposed measures to dilute the Arab population of the Galilee: expanding Jewish settlement, restricting Arab employment and study, and weakening Rakah. Its publication in Al HaMishmar confirmed that demographic management was departmental policy rather than inference.

items.event: Likud's founding platform claims sovereignty between the sea and the Jordan
items.note: The platform of the party that won the 1977 election stated that "between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty" — rendered in the CIA's archived contemporaneous translation of Ma'ariv as "Israel sovereignty alone will prevail between the sea and the Jordan River". The 1999 platform rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state west of the Jordan. Neither has been rescinded.

items.event: Likud takes power; the Drobles Plan sets out settlement to prevent territorial contiguity
items.note: The World Zionist Organisation plan stated the aim of settling between and around Palestinian population centres so as to make a contiguous Palestinian territory impossible.

items.event: Security Council Resolution 446 calls the settlements a violation of the Fourth Geneva Convention
items.note: The Council determined that Israel's settlement policy in the territories occupied since 1967 has no legal validity and constitutes a serious obstruction to peace, and established a commission to examine the situation. The United States abstained; the resolution passed 12–0.

items.event: Egypt–Israel peace treaty
items.note: Removed the strongest Arab military constraint on Israeli action in the occupied territory; the autonomy talks on the Palestinians led nowhere.

items.event: The Elon Moreh judgment bars requisition of private land for settlement
items.note: In Dweikat v. Government of Israel (HCJ 390/79) the Supreme Court held that private Palestinian land could not be seized for a settlement founded on ideological rather than military grounds, and ordered Elon Moreh removed. The state's response was to switch to declaring land public — by 1984 more than 800,000 dunams had been declared state land, and settlement continued on it.

items.event: Jerusalem Law annexes East Jerusalem
items.note: Declared null and void by UN Security Council Resolution 478 in August 1980; the annexation has never been recognised in international law.

items.event: Security Council Resolution 478 declares the Jerusalem Law null and void
items.note: The Council held the Basic Law a violation of international law, declared it null and void, and called on states with diplomatic missions in Jerusalem to withdraw them. Thirteen states did. The resolution is the standing legal answer to the 2017 American recognition.

items.event: Military Order 947 establishes the Civil Administration
items.note: The order created a civil administration in the West Bank under the area commander, separating civil functions from the military government in form while leaving them subordinate to it in substance. It is the body that now issues building permits, demolishes houses and administers land in Area C.

items.event: Security Council Resolution 497 declares the annexation of the Golan without effect
items.note: Adopted unanimously three days after the Golan Heights Law, the resolution held Israel's imposition of its law and administration on the occupied Syrian Golan null and void and without international legal effect, and demanded its rescission. The annexation stands, and was recognised by the United States in March 2019.

items.event: Invasion of Lebanon
items.note: An estimated 17,000–20,000 killed, the great majority civilians, during the invasion and the siege of Beirut.

items.event: The General Assembly calls the Sabra and Shatila massacre an act of genocide
items.note: Resolution 37/123 D resolved that the massacre was an act of genocide, by 123 votes to none with 22 abstentions. It is the only occasion on which the Assembly has applied the term to conduct in this conflict, and it did so three months after the killings and while the Kahan Commission was still sitting.

items.event: Kahan Commission finds Ariel Sharon personally responsible for Sabra and Shatila
items.note: Israel's own commission of inquiry found he bore personal responsibility for ignoring the danger of bloodshed. He resigned as Defence Minister and became Prime Minister eighteen years later.

items.event: The Karp Report is released, two years after it was written
items.note: A committee under Deputy Attorney General Yehudit Karp examined seventy cases of settler violence against Palestinians in 1980–1982 and found fifty-three unsolved, with the police failing to investigate and the army and settlers obstructing. The report was submitted in 1982 and withheld; Karp resigned when nothing was acted on, and the findings have been repeated by every subsequent monitor.

items.event: The 'iron fist' policy in the occupied territory
items.note: Under Defence Minister Yitzhak Rabin: administrative detention restored, deportations resumed on a large scale, and house demolition extended beyond cases of killing or wounding. The UN Special Committee to Investigate Israeli Practices recorded the escalation at the time. Rabin was quoted as saying the purpose was to make life so difficult that the population would leave. The First Intifada began two years later.

items.event: Hamas is founded in Gaza
items.note: Formed out of the Muslim Brotherhood's Gaza branch in the first days of the intifada. Israel had permitted and in part encouraged the Brotherhood's charitable and religious network through the 1970s and 1980s as a counterweight to the secular nationalism of the PLO — a calculation Israeli officials have since acknowledged in print.

items.event: The 'force, might and beatings' policy in the First Intifada
items.note: Defence Minister Yitzhak Rabin's instruction; some 1,000 Palestinians hospitalised with fractures in the first months, documented at the time by Israeli and international medical organisations.

items.event: Jordan severs its legal and administrative ties to the West Bank
items.note: King Hussein's address dissolved the Jordanian parliament's West Bank seats and ended the administrative link, leaving the PLO as the sole claimant. The Palestinian Declaration of Independence followed in November, and the West Bank's residents were left holding no citizenship at all.

items.event: Palestinian Declaration of Independence accepts partition on the 1967 lines
items.note: The PLO's acceptance of a state on 22% of historic Palestine. Recognised within a year by more than 80 states.

items.event: Al-Aqsa compound killings: 21 Palestinians shot dead
items.note: UN Security Council Resolution 672 condemned the killings; Israel refused entry to the Secretary-General's mission.

items.event: The Madrid conference opens
items.note: The first direct multilateral talks, convened by the United States and the Soviet Union. The PLO was excluded by Israeli veto and the Palestinians attended inside a joint Jordanian delegation. The conference produced no agreement; the channel that produced Oslo was opened secretly alongside it.

items.event: 415 Palestinians are deported to Marj al-Zuhour
items.note: The mass expulsion of alleged Hamas and Islamic Jihad members to a strip of southern Lebanon, where they were refused entry and spent a winter in tents. The Security Council condemned it as a violation of the Fourth Geneva Convention in Resolution 799 the following day and demanded their safe and immediate return; most returned in 1993.

items.event: Oslo I: Declaration of Principles signed in Washington
items.note: Deferred Jerusalem, refugees, settlements and borders to final-status talks that never concluded. The settler population roughly doubled during the Oslo years.

items.event: The Paris Protocol binds the Palestinian economy to Israel's
items.note: The economic annex of the Oslo framework created a customs union in which Israel collects Palestinian import duties and VAT and transfers them, sets the tariff schedule, and controls the crossings. The clearance revenues so collected have been withheld repeatedly since, which is why the arrangement is described as a lever rather than a partnership.

items.event: The Gaza–Jericho Agreement begins the transfer of civil powers
items.note: Signed in Cairo, it created the Palestinian Authority and moved Israeli forces out of Jericho and most of Gaza, while leaving settlements, borders, airspace and external security with Israel. The interim arrangements it set up for five years are still in force.

items.event: Oslo II divides the West Bank into Areas A, B and C
items.note: Area C, some 60% of the West Bank and the location of nearly all its land reserves, remained under full Israeli control — an arrangement intended to last five years and still in force after thirty.

items.event: Yitzhak Rabin assassinated by Yigal Amir
items.note: Killed by an Israeli religious-nationalist opposed to the Oslo Accords, after a campaign of incitement in which Benjamin Netanyahu was a prominent figure.

items.event: Hebron Protocol divides the city into H1 and H2
items.note: 80% of Hebron transferred to the Palestinian Authority; the 20% containing the Old City, the Ibrahimi Mosque, four settlements and Shuhada Street kept under Israeli control, where some 7,000 Palestinians live alongside 500–800 settlers and about 1,500 soldiers. The Protocol required Shuhada Street to be reopened; it was fenced off entirely in 2002 and Palestinians remain barred from it. Smotrich announced the Protocol's cancellation in June 2026.

items.event: Wye River Memorandum
items.note: A further redeployment agreement brokered at Wye Plantation; implementation was suspended by Israel two months later. The last of the Oslo-era agreements before the collapse at Camp David.

items.event: The Supreme Court holds that the interrogation methods are unlawful
items.note: In PCATI v. State of Israel (HCJ 5100/94) the court ruled that shaking, the shabach position, painful squatting and sleep deprivation were not authorised by law, while leaving open a necessity defence for individual interrogators after the fact. The defence became the route by which the practices continued; the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel records that almost no complaint has resulted in a prosecution since.

items.event: Camp David summit collapses
items.note: The 'generous offer' narrative that followed is contradicted by the accounts of participants, including US negotiator Robert Malley and Israeli negotiator Shlomo Ben-Ami.

items.event: The Mitchell Committee reports on the second intifada
items.note: The international fact-finding committee chaired by Senator George Mitchell called for an unconditional ceasefire, a freeze on all settlement construction including natural growth, and an end to Palestinian attacks. The settlement freeze was not implemented; the committee's finding that the Palestinian Authority had not planned the uprising is also part of the record.

items.event: The Arab League adopts the Arab Peace Initiative at the Beirut summit
items.note: Proposed by Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah bin Abdulaziz and adopted at the Fourteenth Arab Summit. Paragraph 2 asks Israel to affirm withdrawal from the territories occupied since 1967 "to the lines of 4 June 1967", a just solution to the refugee question under UNGA Resolution 194, and a sovereign Palestinian state "with East Jerusalem as its capital". Paragraph 3 states what the Arab states undertake in return: to "Consider the Arab-Israeli conflict ended, enter into a peace agreement with Israel, and provide security for all the states of the region", and to "Establish normal relations with Israel in the context of this comprehensive peace". Re-endorsed at Riyadh in 2007 and at the Dead Sea summit in Jordan in March 2017. No Israeli government has accepted it as a basis for negotiation; in June 2016 Haaretz reported Netanyahu telling Likud ministers that if it were brought as take it or leave it, Israel would "choose to leave it". It remains the only peace offer agreed by the League as a body.

items.event: Operation Defensive Shield: reoccupation of the West Bank cities
items.note: The Palestinian Authority's institutions were destroyed and Area A reoccupied; the arrangement of raids into Area A continues to this day.

items.event: Construction of the separation wall begins
items.note: About 85% of its route runs inside the West Bank rather than on the Green Line, enclosing major settlement blocs. Ruled contrary to international law by the ICJ in 2004.

items.event: The Quartet publishes the Road Map
items.note: A three-phase plan to a Palestinian state by 2005, with a settlement freeze in phase one. Israel accepted it with fourteen reservations; the state did not arrive, the freeze did not happen, and the settler population of the West Bank roughly doubled over the following two decades.

items.event: The Citizenship and Entry into Israel Law bars family unification with Palestinian spouses
items.note: Enacted as a temporary order, the law prevents Palestinian citizens of Israel who marry Palestinians from the West Bank or Gaza from living with their spouses in Israel. It was upheld by a divided Supreme Court in 2006 and again in 2012, lapsed briefly in 2021, was re-enacted in 2022, and has been renewed year on year for more than two decades. Adalah records it as the clearest instance of a measure directed at one group by nationality and applied indefinitely under a temporary heading.

items.event: The Beit Sourik judgment orders the wall's route changed
items.note: In Beit Sourik Village Council v. Government of Israel (HCJ 2056/04) the Supreme Court accepted the security rationale for the barrier but held some thirty kilometres of its route disproportionate in the harm done to the villagers, and ordered it moved. The International Court of Justice gave its advisory opinion nine days later, holding the sections inside occupied territory contrary to international law altogether.

items.event: Disengagement: settlers and soldiers withdrawn from inside Gaza
items.note: Israel retained control of Gaza's airspace, territorial waters, population registry and all but one crossing; the UN, the ICRC and the ICJ continue to treat Gaza as occupied territory.

items.event: Hamas wins the Palestinian legislative elections
items.note: Monitored and certified as free and fair by international observers, including the Carter Center and the EU. Aid was suspended and the blockade followed.

items.event: Israel's Camp David foreign minister says he would have rejected the offer
items.note: Shlomo Ben-Ami, who led the Israeli delegation at Camp David and Taba, tells Democracy Now!: 'Camp David was not the missed opportunity for the Palestinians, and if I were a Palestinian I would have rejected Camp David, as well.' In the same exchange he holds Arafat responsible for the later response to the Clinton Parameters. Rebuttal 21.

items.event: The Lebanon war begins
items.note: Thirty-four days of fighting that killed about 1,100 Lebanese, most of them civilians, and 165 Israelis. Israel's air force chief described the Dahiya doctrine that emerged from it — disproportionate force against the civilian infrastructure of the area from which fire comes — a doctrine later cited in relation to Gaza by the Goldstone Report.

items.event: The ICJ rules on the duty to prevent genocide in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro
items.note: The only judgment to date on Article I of the Genocide Convention. The Court held that a state's obligation to prevent arises "at the instant that the State learns of, or should normally have learned of, the existence of a serious risk that genocide will be committed", that it is an obligation of conduct and not of result — breached where a state "manifestly failed to take all measures to prevent genocide which were within its power" — and that whether the effort would have succeeded is irrelevant (paragraphs 430–431). It is the authority under which waiting for a final determination is itself the breach.

items.event: The Annapolis conference relaunches final-status talks
items.note: Convened by the United States with Israeli, Palestinian and Arab participation, it set a target of an agreement by the end of 2008. The talks ended with the Gaza offensive of December 2008; Olmert's map, offered in September 2008, was the last final-status proposal made.

items.event: Olmert shows Abbas a map and will not let him keep it
items.note: Ehud Olmert proposes that Israel retain 6.3 per cent of the West Bank against a 5.8 per cent swap, with a link to Gaza and the Old City under an international regime; he shows Mahmoud Abbas the map but refuses a copy, and an aide reproduces it from memory. Olmert submits his resignation five days later, under criminal investigation. Rebuttal 21.

items.event: Goldstone Report documents the Dahiya Doctrine
items.note: The UN fact-finding mission on the 2008–09 Gaza conflict found evidence of war crimes and possible crimes against humanity, and recorded the deliberate application of disproportionate force against civilian infrastructure as doctrine.

items.event: The Knesset passes the anti-boycott law, 47 to 38
items.note: The Law for Prevention of Damage to the State of Israel through Boycott creates civil liability for calling for a boycott of the state or of the settlements. In Avneri v. Knesset (HCJ 5239/11, 15 April 2015) the Supreme Court struck down only section 2(c), which had allowed damages without proof of harm, and upheld the rest. Rebuttal 22.

items.event: UNESCO admits Palestine as a member state
items.note: The vote was 107 to 14 with 52 abstentions. The United States and Israel cut their funding of the agency in response, under American statutes barring contributions to any UN body admitting Palestine, and both later withdrew from it.

items.event: UN General Assembly recognises Palestine as a non-member observer state
items.note: 138 votes in favour. The status that made accession to the Rome Statute possible.

items.event: Palestine accedes to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court
items.note: The jurisdictional basis for the ICC investigation and for the arrest warrants of November 2024.

items.event: Settlers firebomb the Dawabsheh family home in Duma, killing 18-month-old Ali Dawabsheh and both his parents
items.note: Hebrew graffiti reading “Revenge!” was left at the scene; a second, empty house in the village was firebombed the same night. The couple's five-year-old son Ahmed survived with severe burns.

items.event: UN Security Council Resolution 2334 declares the settlements a flagrant violation of international law
items.note: Adopted 14–0 with the United States abstaining — the only occasion in the period on which a settlement resolution was not vetoed.

items.event: The ESCWA apartheid report is published and withdrawn
items.note: The report by Richard Falk and Virginia Tilley for the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia concluded that Israel had established an apartheid regime. Under American and Israeli pressure the Secretary-General ordered it removed from the commission's website, and the commission's executive secretary, Rima Khalaf, resigned rather than comply.

items.event: The United States recognises Jerusalem as Israel's capital
items.note: Condemned by the General Assembly 128–9. The embassy moved on 14 May 2018, the day Israeli forces killed some 60 Palestinians at the Gaza perimeter fence.

items.event: The United States moves its embassy to Jerusalem
items.note: The opening ceremony was held on the seventieth anniversary of the declaration of the state. On the same day, Israeli forces shot dead about sixty demonstrators at the Gaza perimeter fence during the Great March of Return; the UN Human Rights Council's commission of inquiry later found that the shootings were of unarmed protesters and may amount to crimes against humanity.

items.event: REFORM Alliance founded in New York by Michael Rubin, Jay-Z, Meek Mill, Robert Kraft, Clara Wu Tsai, Daniel Loeb, Michael Novogratz and Robert F. Smith, with a combined pledge of fifty million dollars and Van Jones as chief executive.
items.note: The documented association behind the photographs of Kraft with those figures circulated after the September 2026 removal of Macklemore from the Loop Tour. Recorded at §15.12.

items.event: The United States declares that settlements are 'not per se inconsistent with international law'
items.note: The Pompeo declaration reversed the 1978 Hansell opinion of the State Department's own legal adviser. It was reversed again in 2024, and the settlements' status in international law was unaffected throughout.

items.event: Israel deports the Human Rights Watch director
items.note: Omar Shakir, the organisation's Israel and Palestine director, was expelled after the Supreme Court upheld the order on 5 November under the 2017 amendment to the Entry to Israel Law barring anyone who has called for a boycott. The court held that the bar applies even where the call is founded on the protection of human rights or on international law; it was the first expulsion under the amendment.

items.event: The ICC Prosecutor finds a basis to investigate
items.note: Fatou Bensouda concluded the five-year preliminary examination with the determination that war crimes have been or are being committed in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and in Gaza, that cases would be admissible, and that an investigation would serve the interests of justice. She asked the Pre-Trial Chamber to confirm the territorial scope first; the investigation opened on 3 March 2021.

items.event: Lod District Court convicts Amiram Ben-Uliel of the Duma murders and classifies the offences as a terrorist act
items.note: Three counts of murder, two of attempted murder and conspiracy; three life sentences and twenty further years; motive found to be “extreme and racist ideology”. Acquitted of membership of a terrorist organisation. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in 2022. A later crowdfunding campaign for his release raised more than NIS 1.2 million, and fourteen coalition lawmakers signed a petition to improve his prison conditions.

items.event: The European Court of Human Rights rules the call for a boycott is protected expression
items.note: Baldassi and Others v. France: unanimous finding that the criminal conviction of eleven activists for calling for a boycott of Israeli goods violated Article 10, with EUR 7,380 awarded to each. The Court distinguished Willem v. France (2009), where the applicant acted as a mayor exercising public authority. Rebuttal 22.

items.event: Abraham Accords signed
items.note: Normalisation with the UAE and Bahrain, in exchange for the suspension rather than the abandonment of the West Bank annexation plan.

items.event: ICC Prosecutor opens the investigation into the situation in Palestine
items.note: Covering conduct in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza since 13 June 2014.

items.event: The Supreme Court upholds the Nation State Basic Law, ten to one
items.note: An extended bench of eleven justices rejected fifteen petitions against Basic Law: Israel — the Nation State of the Jewish People. President Esther Hayut held that the law did not negate the state's democratic character. The sole dissent was that of Justice George Karra, the court's only Arab justice. The judgment is the answer to the argument that representation inside Israeli institutions is itself a check on the law's constitutional hierarchy.

items.event: Kraft Group LLC gives $1,000,000 to the United Democracy Project, AIPAC's super political action committee
items.note: The first of five disclosed contributions from the Kraft Group to the committee, which reach $3,000,000 by 26 February 2026 and place the entity sixth among its private contributors. Recorded in the Federal Election Commission's itemised receipts (committee C00799031).

items.event: The most right-wing government in Israel's history takes office
items.note: Itamar Ben-Gvir at National Security and Bezalel Smotrich at Finance with authority over the Civil Administration in the West Bank. Its coalition agreement asserted an exclusive and inalienable Jewish right to all of the Land of Israel.

items.event: 2022 is the deadliest year for West Bank Palestinians since OCHA records began in 2005
items.note: 155 killed, including 36 children (OCHA); B'Tselem counted 146 killed by Israeli forces, the largest number since 2004. The record stood for one year.

items.event: Huwara: hundreds of settlers burn homes and cars; Smotrich says the village 'needs to be wiped out'
items.note: The IDF general commanding the West Bank called it a pogrom. Smotrich, the minister with authority over the Civil Administration, said the state should do the wiping out.

items.event: 104 organisations, among them B'Tselem and Breaking the Silence, ask the United Nations not to adopt the IHRA definition
items.note: Open letter to Secretary-General António Guterres and High Representative Miguel Ángel Moratinos, signed by sixty organisations on 3 April and by 104 by 20 April 2023. It states that antisemitism “poses real harm to Jewish communities around the world and requires meaningful action to combat it”, and objects that the IHRA working definition “has often been used to wrongly label criticism of Israel as antisemitic”. It names the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism and the Nexus Document as alternatives. Signatories include Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, the ACLU, Al-Haq and FIDH, together with the Israeli organisations B'Tselem and Breaking the Silence and the American Jewish organisation Americans for Peace Now. A counter-letter of 17 May 2023, signed by more than 160 Jewish communal and civil society organisations, urged the opposite course, calling the definition “an indispensable tool”. See §21.9.

items.event: Two-day assault on Jenin refugee camp
items.note: The largest West Bank operation since 2002: air strikes, bulldozed infrastructure and some 3,000 displaced, three months before the war.

items.event: 208 Palestinians killed in the West Bank before 7 October, including 42 children
items.note: 2023 was already the deadliest year on record in the West Bank before the war began (OCHA).

items.event: The Saint Porphyrius compound is struck
items.note: An Israeli strike hit a building adjoining the Greek Orthodox church in Gaza City, where about 500 displaced Muslims and Christians were sheltering. The standard count is 18 killed; Airwars identified at least 23 civilians by name, including ten children, eight women and five men of the al-Amash, al-Souri and al-Tarazi families. The Israeli military said it had struck a Hamas command and control centre and that the church was not the target. The original fabric of the building dates to 425 AD.

items.event: Nahida and Samar Anton are shot inside the Holy Family parish
items.note: Nahida Khalil Anton, 70, and her daughter Samar Kamal Anton, 50, were shot dead while walking inside the grounds of Gaza's only Catholic parish, which was sheltering 648 people. The Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa, stated that "a sniper of the IDF murdered two Christian women inside the Holy Family Parish in Gaza" and that seven more were wounded as they tried to shield others, with no warning given. The Israeli military denied targeting civilians and, in the account carried by Vatican News, asserted that a rocket launcher was present in the parish; no evidence for that assertion has been produced since.

items.event: Netanyahu states that he will not compromise on control west of the Jordan
items.note: At a press conference the prime minister said he "will not compromise on full Israeli security control over all the territory west of the Jordan River", repeating a formulation he had used since 2017 and setting it out again in the "day after" plan he published the following month. The same territorial formulation, in other mouths, has produced censures and suspensions.

items.event: Jonathan Glazer refuses the use of Jewishness and the Holocaust to justify the war, accepting an Academy Award
items.note: More than a thousand Jewish film-industry figures signed a letter denouncing the speech; more than 150, including Joaquin Phoenix, Joel Coen, Nan Goldin, Tom Stoppard and Elliott Gould, signed one supporting it (§23.4).

items.event: More than eighty acts and speakers withdraw from SXSW over the US Army sponsorship
items.note: The Austin For Palestine Coalition initiated the boycott over the festival's listing of the United States Army as a "super sponsor" and the involvement of RTX, Collins Aerospace and BAE Systems. SXSW announced that the Army and the named weapons manufacturers would not sponsor its 2025 edition.

items.event: The ICJ orders additional provisional measures as famine sets in
items.note: Finding that conditions had deteriorated since January, the Court ordered Israel to take all necessary and effective measures to ensure the unimpeded provision of basic services and humanitarian assistance at scale, including food, water, fuel and medical supplies, and to ensure its military does not violate the rights of Palestinians under the Convention.

items.event: An Israeli Holocaust historian publishes the genocide finding in Hebrew
items.note: Amos Goldberg, professor of Holocaust history at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, publishes "Yes, it is genocide" in Sicha Mekomit (Local Call), the first such determination written in Hebrew for an Israeli readership: "Yes, it is genocide. It is so difficult and painful to admit it, but despite all that, and despite all our efforts to think otherwise, after six months of brutal war we can no longer avoid this conclusion." Sol Salbe's English translation follows the next day. The UN Commission of Inquiry reaches the same conclusion on the full evidentiary standard seventeen months later.

items.event: Israeli historian Ilan Pappé detained and questioned for two hours at Detroit airport
items.note: Asked whether he supported Hamas, whether he regarded the assault on Gaza as genocide, and to name his Arab and Muslim friends in the United States; released after the contents of his telephone were copied. Pappé later clarified that the questioning agency was the Department of Homeland Security, not the FBI as first reported (§23.3).

items.event: 126 acts withdraw from The Great Escape over Barclays sponsorship
items.note: More than a quarter of the line-up by the festival's opening day; organisers put the final figure at 151. The Bands Boycott Barclays campaign cited the bank's holdings in suppliers to the Israeli military. Barclays ceased to be a partner of the festival from 2025.

items.event: The ICJ orders the Rafah offensive halted
items.note: The Court ordered Israel to halt immediately its military offensive in Rafah, to keep the Rafah crossing open for humanitarian assistance at scale, and to admit investigators mandated to examine allegations of genocide. The offensive continued.

items.event: The State of Israel's official account publishes the Ed Sheeran photograph
items.note: The official Instagram account of the State of Israel, @stateofisrael, published the backstage photograph taken at the Global Citizen Festival in Central Park on 28 September 2024, in which Ed Sheeran appears with Noa Argamani, the Israeli hostage held for 246 days and rescued on 8 June 2024, who attended as a guest of the music executive Scooter Braun. The caption read "We ❤️ this so much." and recorded that "Former hostage Noa Argamani met Ed Sheeran and Post Malone". The post carries approximately 60,400 likes and 852 comments and recirculated widely after Macklemore's removal from the Loop Tour on 14 September 2026. The photograph is not a political act by the artist and the attendance of a released hostage is not a political act either; what is recorded is the use made of it by a party to the conflict, which bears on the ground stated on 15 September 2026 that his silence should not be read as complicity (§15.12).

items.event: The US Treasury designates Hilltop Youth, treating violent West Bank settlers as an organised group
items.note: The designation under Executive Order 14115 describes a campaign of "killings, arson, assaults, and intimidation" intended to drive Palestinian communities out of the West Bank, citing the attacks on Turmus Ayya in June 2023 and al-Mughayyir in April 2024. The United Kingdom, the European Union, Canada, Australia and Japan took materially similar measures, several of them also naming Lehava.

items.event: Executive Order 14115 is revoked and the settler sanctions are lifted
items.note: On his first day in office President Trump revoked the order under which the settler designations were made; on 24 January 2025 OFAC removed 17 Israeli individuals, nine entities and six outposts from the Specially Designated Nationals list. Marco Rubio had confirmed the intention at his confirmation hearing days earlier. The designations had described the conduct; the revocation removed the consequence, not the finding.

items.event: Israel resumes bombing while the January ceasefire's terms are being observed
items.note: More than 400 people killed in a single night, the deadliest day since October 2023. Phase one had run to 1 March with its exchanges completed in eight rounds; the phase two negotiations the agreement required to open on the sixteenth day were never opened, and all goods had been halted on 2 March. Rebuttal 19.

items.event: 1,137 UK lawyers, legal academics and former judges sign an open letter on the Occupied Palestinian Territory
items.note: The signatories, including former Supreme Court Justices Lord Sumption and Lord Wilson, state that 'genocide is being perpetrated in Gaza or, at a minimum, there is a serious risk of genocide occurring' and that 'The UK's actions to date have failed to meet those standards.'

items.event: The Gaza Humanitarian Foundation begins distributing aid
items.note: Four militarised sites, secured by armed private United States contractors inside Israeli-controlled perimeters, replaced the roughly 400 distribution points the UN-coordinated system had run during the ceasefire. UNRWA's Commissioner-General described the change as going from four hundred points to four. OHCHR went on to record the killing of people trying to collect food near those sites and along convoy routes: 613 by 27 June, 798 by 7 July, 1,373 by 31 July and more than 2,146 by 4 September 2025.

items.event: Defence Minister Israel Katz orders preparation of a sealed “humanitarian city” on the ruins of Rafah
items.note: An initial 600,000 displaced Palestinians from al-Mawasi, and eventually the whole population of Gaza, to be admitted after screening and not permitted to leave except by emigrating from the Strip.

items.event: Two former Israeli prime ministers call the Rafah plan a concentration camp; the army declines to execute it
items.note: Ehud Olmert: “It is a concentration camp. I am sorry.” Yair Lapid, conditionally, the same day. Sixteen Israeli law academics had written on 10 July that any order to advance the plan was manifestly illegal; the Chief of the General Staff told the High Court the army “does not impose forced population expulsions”. The plan was later reported shelved.

items.event: The Holy Family Church is struck
items.note: An Israeli munition hit Gaza's only Catholic church, where about 600 people were sheltering, killing Saad Salama, the 60-year-old parish janitor, Fumya Ayaad, 84, and Najwa Abu Dawood, 71, and injuring ten including the parish priest, Father Gabriel Romanelli. Prime Minister Netanyahu's office said Israel "deeply regrets that a stray ammunition hit Gaza's Holy Family Church" and the Foreign Ministry said the findings would be "published transparently"; survivors described a strike without warning and no published investigation has been identified since. Cardinal Pizzaballa and Patriarch Theophilos III entered Gaza together the following day.

items.event: A United States review finds no evidence that Hamas systematically diverted American-funded aid
items.note: Reuters reported an internal analysis by USAID's humanitarian bureau, completed in late June 2025, which examined 156 incidents of theft or loss of United States-funded supplies reported by partners between October 2023 and May 2025 and found no report alleging that Hamas had benefited. The analysis records that it could not assess whether recipients had been vetted. It is the rationale for the new distribution model, tested against the government's own record.

items.event: The Royal Ballet and Opera cancels its 2026 Tosca in Tel Aviv after 182 staff sign an open letter
items.note: Chief executive Alex Beard told staff the production "will not be going to Israel." The letter, signed by 182 members of the company with 40 in their own names, stated "We reject any current or future performances in Israel" and, on the contrast with the institution's response to the invasion of Ukraine, "The double standard is deafening."

items.event: Six journalists are killed in a strike on a media tent outside al-Shifa Hospital
items.note: Anas al-Sharif, Mohammed Qreiqeh, Ibrahim Zaher, Mohammed Noufal, Moamen Aliwa and Mohammad al-Khaldi were killed by a drone strike on a tent used by the press. The Israeli military said it had struck "the terrorist Anas Al-Sharif, who posed as a journalist"; no case was offered for the other five. The Committee to Protect Journalists had warned a month earlier that al-Sharif was the subject of a smear campaign. More than 190 journalists and media workers have been killed since October 2023.

items.event: Fourteen of the fifteen Security Council members issue a joint statement on the famine
items.note: Five days after the IPC confirmed famine in Gaza Governorate, every member of the Council except the United States signed a joint statement on the classification. The United Nations humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, called the evidence "irrefutable testimony", adding: "It is a famine, the Gaza famine."

items.event: Film Workers for Palestine publishes a pledge not to work with Israeli film institutions implicated in genocide and apartheid, naming the Jerusalem and Haifa festivals, Docaviv and TLVFest; signatures pass 1,300 on the first day and 5,000 in the weeks following.
items.note: Signatories include Olivia Colman, Emma Stone, Tilda Swinton, Riz Ahmed, Ava DuVernay, Joaquin Phoenix, Javier Bardem, Ken Loach and Mark Ruffalo. Recorded at §15.12A.

items.event: Together for Palestine, a benefit concert organised by Brian Eno, sells out the 12,500-capacity OVO Arena Wembley and raises a reported £2 million, distributed by Choose Love to Palestinian-led organisations.
items.note: Speakers included Florence Pugh, Nicola Coughlan, Benedict Cumberbatch, Mehdi Hasan, Eric Cantona and UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese. No objection from the venue's owner was reported. Recorded at §15.12A.

items.event: No Music For Genocide launches, asking artists to geo-block their catalogues in Israel
items.note: More than 400 artists and labels joined at launch, passing 1,000 by November 2025. Participants include Massive Attack, Björk, Lorde, Fontaines D.C., Primal Scream and Kneecap.

items.event: Trump's twenty-point Gaza plan published, with Point 19 describing statehood as an aspiration rather than a right
items.note: Point 19 states that once redevelopment advances and Palestinian Authority reform is carried out, "the conditions may finally be in place for a credible pathway to Palestinian self-determination and statehood, which we recognize as the aspiration of the Palestinian people". Neither Point 19 nor Point 20 mentions the West Bank. The Security Council endorsed the plan in Resolution 2803 on 17 November 2025.

items.event: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio declines to affirm support for a Palestinian state on CBS's Face the Nation
items.note: Asked by Margaret Brennan about Point 19, Rubio said statehood could come only through a negotiated deal with Israel, that the United States "hasn't recognized" a Palestinian state and there is "no point in doing that" because it is not "even a realistic thing right now", and that Point 19 describes "a pathway long term and in the future" from which "we are far". Brennan reported that off camera he had clarified that President Trump still opposes Israeli annexation of the West Bank.

items.event: The Knesset gives preliminary approval to two West Bank annexation bills by 25 votes to 24
items.note: One bill would apply Israeli sovereignty to all West Bank settlements, the other to Ma'ale Adumim; Netanyahu reportedly told Likud members to abstain, and the bills faced further readings they were not expected to survive. The vote fell during Vice-President J.D. Vance's visit, who called it an insult to administration policy and said the West Bank will not be annexed; Rubio said the next day it was "not something we can be supportive of right now".

items.event: The Gaza Humanitarian Foundation winds up its operations
items.note: The foundation closed after six months, having been called on to shut down by more than 165 humanitarian organisations. The distribution model it was created to replace — the UN-coordinated network of some 400 points — had been operating without the casualty toll recorded at its sites.

items.event: Netanyahu thanks the chairman of the Los Angeles Olympics
items.note: The Israeli Prime Minister's Office published a readout of a meeting in Jerusalem with Casey Wasserman, chairperson of the LA28 organising committee and founder of the agency that represents Ed Sheeran, Coldplay and Kendrick Lamar for live performance, recording that Netanyahu "congratulated Chairman Wasserman on his visit to Israel and thanked him for his great support for the State of Israel." The meeting took place three months after the UN Commission of Inquiry found genocide and thirteen months after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu. Wasserman also met President Herzog, visited Kibbutz Be'eri and told the Israeli Olympic Committee that the security of the Israeli delegation was his "number one concern".

items.event: EU High Representative Kaja Kallas sets out the Gaza obstruction in paired terms in Egypt
items.note: Hamas 'refuses to disarm, blocking progress towards the next stages of the peace plan' while 'at the same time Israel is restricting international NGOs, seriously jeopardising access to humanitarian aid.'

items.event: Survey finds a third of American Jews identify as Zionist and 7 per cent as anti-Zionist
items.note: Jewish Federations of North America / Burson, fielded March 2025 among more than 1,800 Jewish respondents: nearly nine in ten support Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, 71 per cent report emotional attachment, and the anti-Zionist share rises to 14 per cent among those aged 18–34 (§23.5).

items.event: UK Divisional Court holds the proscription of Palestine Action unlawful and disproportionate
items.note: R (Ammori) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2026] EWHC 292 (Admin), before Dame Victoria Sharp P, Swift J and Steyn J. The decision was taken outside the Home Secretary's own policy, and the interference with Articles 10 and 11 ECHR was disproportionate: "A very small number of Palestine Action's activities amounted to acts of terrorism within the definition of section 1 of the 2000 Act." The ban stayed in force pending argument on a stay.

items.event: The Epstein files release reaches the music agency
items.note: The Department of Justice release made under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, more than three million documents, contained 2003 correspondence between Casey Wasserman and Ghislaine Maxwell and records of a flight on Epstein's aircraft. Wasserman has not been accused of any wrongdoing and said he deeply regrets the correspondence. Chappell Roan, Orville Peck, Weyes Blood, Laufey, bbno$, Gigi Perez and Abby Wambach left the agency; on 13 February he wrote to staff that he had "become a distraction" and had begun the process of selling the company. The Mayor of Los Angeles called on him to resign from the Olympic role; he said he intends to remain.

items.event: Churchill statue in Parliament Square painted with “Free Palestine” and “Zionist war criminal”; one arrest
items.note: A man climbs the plinth before 4am and paints the statue, then tells the arriving officers he wanted to be arrested. He is held on suspicion of racially aggravated criminal damage and of supporting the proscribed Palestine Action, and is charged with a single count of criminal damage.

items.event: SIPRI records the supply relationship behind the transfers
items.note: SIPRI's Trends in International Arms Transfers, 2025 put the United States at 42 per cent of global exports of major arms for 2021-25, up from 36 per cent in 2016-20, and recorded that the United States supplied 68 per cent of Israel's imports of major arms in the same period, with Germany supplying 31 per cent. Israel was itself the world's seventh largest exporter at 4.4 per cent. SIPRI noted that supplier states continued transfers throughout the period despite stated concern about the civilian death toll in Gaza and about violations of international law.

items.event: Rossing Center records 155 attacks on Christians in Israel and East Jerusalem in 2025
items.note: Third annual report of the Israeli organisation: 61 physical assaults, 52 attacks on church property, 28 cases of verbal harassment and 14 defacements of Christian signage, against 111 incidents in 2024 and 89 in 2023. The Religious Freedom Data Center counted 181 incidents independently, more than 80 per cent of them in Jerusalem.

items.event: The Knesset passes the Death Penalty for Terrorists Law, 62 votes to 48
items.note: Mandatory death by hanging before military courts, which try Palestinians alone; execution within 90 days of final judgment; no mitigation, commutation or pardon; the civilian-track offence is confined to killing aimed at "denying the existence of the State of Israel", which keeps Jewish attackers outside its reach. Initiated by Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit; Netanyahu voted for it in person. Petitions were filed the same day by ACRI and by Adalah with PCATI, HaMoked, PHR-Israel and Gisha.

items.event: UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination finds the Israeli death penalty law racially discriminatory
items.note: The CERD statement, released 1 May 2026, calls the law a grave human rights retrogression and an instance of segregation, notes that it applies de facto to Palestinians only, and calls on all States parties to ensure their own resources are not used to enforce discriminatory policies in the occupied territory. Israel ratified the Convention in 1979.

items.event: The Jerusalem Day flag march passes through the Muslim Quarter under police protection
items.note: The Associated Press recorded crowds chanting "Death to Arabs" and "May your villages burn" as they marched through the occupied Old City, with Israeli police cordoning the route. Israeli reporters recorded further chants, assaults on journalists, and notices taped to cash machines reading "Jewish owned, do not torch". Settlers burned a mosque and vehicles at Jibiya near Ramallah the same night. The march is authorised and policed annually.

items.event: The Israeli Central Command commander signs the order bringing the death penalty law into force in the West Bank
items.note: The order extends the mandatory capital sentence to the military courts of the occupied West Bank, whose conviction rate B'Tselem puts at about 96 per cent, very substantially on the basis of confessions obtained in interrogation.

items.event: Global Echo Litigation Center publishes Importing Occupation on settlement goods in European supply chains
items.note: More than 30,000 Israeli export documents analysed: over 17 per cent of 5,900 shipments to Europe between October 2017 and February 2026 carried settlement-origin products labelled Product of Israel.

items.event: The Court of Appeal reverses the Palestine Action judgment and restores the proscription
items.note: Secretary of State for the Home Department v Ammori [2026] EWCA Civ 1721, a five-member court including the Lady Chief Justice and the Master of the Rolls. National-security risk assessment is "pre-eminently a question of specialist evaluation and judgement for the executive"; proscription left the "core or essence" of lawful expression "untouched"; the case was nonetheless "borderline".

items.event: Israel severs all contact with Kaja Kallas over a reported apartheid comparison
items.note: Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said he had 'no choice but to sever all contact' unless she withdrew what he called a 'blood libel'; Kallas replied without disputing the report.

items.event: The UK Supreme Court grants Huda Ammori permission to appeal against the Palestine Action proscription
items.note: The appeal is expected to be heard before the end of 2026; prosecutions arising from the ban were adjourned to 26 October 2026. The organisation remains proscribed and support for it remains a terrorism offence. Ammori has cited more than 3,500 arrests connected with the proscription.

items.event: Employment Appeal Tribunal holds that an anti-Zionist belief is protected under the Equality Act 2010
items.note: University of Bristol v Dr David Miller [2026] EAT 84 (EA-2024-000324-RS). Eight of the university’s nine grounds of appeal were rejected, leaving standing the Bristol tribunal’s finding of 6 February 2024 that the belief satisfies the Grainger criteria under s. 10 and that the dismissal was direct discrimination under s. 13. The protection attaches to the bounded formulation Miller advanced, not to anti-Zionism at large.

items.event: The Charity Commission opens a statutory class inquiry into British charities working in illegal Israeli settlements
items.note: The regulator for England and Wales opened a fact-finding inquiry under section 46 of the Charities Act 2011, beginning with eight unnamed charities and stating that it intends to extend the number over time. It followed a complaint in June 2026 by the Labour MP Melanie Ward alleging that 32 charities had sent at least £28 million to settlements, up to £5.6 million of it subsidised by the taxpayer through Gift Aid. The Commission stressed that opening an inquiry is not a finding of wrongdoing, and shared the scope with the police and HM Revenue and Customs. Recorded at §15.3A.

items.event: Publication of Israel's Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power, by Eli Clifton and Ian S. Lustick (Atria/One Signal).
items.note: Traces privately funded advocacy through donor-advised funds and comparable vehicles, outside the reach of the FARA test set out in Part XX.

items.event: The Supreme Court of New South Wales rejects the IHRA definition as “detached from … reality”
items.note: State of New South Wales v Farhat [2026] NSWSC 985, decided 30 July 2026 with reasons published 17 August. Refusing an extended supervision order under the Terrorism (High Risk Offenders) Act 2017 (NSW), Fagan J held the IHRA working definition “so verbose and imprecise that it could not realistically be attributed to the ordinary, reasonably informed member of the Australian public”, an attempt “to repurpose the term ‘antisemitism’”, and “detached from the reality of the common usage and understanding of antisemitism in this country”. On 31 August 2026 the New South Wales Attorney General, Michael Daley, said the State would not appeal. See §21.9.

items.event: Al Jazeera and Tussell identify 2.129 billion pounds in UK public-sector contracts with settlement-linked companies
items.note: 17 companies hold 125 contracts; five Motorola Solutions entities account for 1.726 billion pounds, including a 1.562 billion pound Home Office emergency-services network contract held by Airwave Solutions.

items.event: Portuguese acts withdraw from a Lisbon comedy festival headlined by Jerry Seinfeld
items.note: Inês Aires Pereira withdrew her 29 October show, saying "we cannot relativise or normalise a genocide"; the duo Cebola Mol withdrew the same day. Earlier cancellations included the Tributo Pop show and Conjunto Cuca Monga.

items.event: Zeteo publishes a debate between Peter Beinart and Joel Rubin, moderated by Mehdi Hasan, on antisemitism and anti-Zionism
items.note: Rubin: “Anti-Zionists are clearly hostile to the idea that the state of Israel should exist.” Beinart: “There's a very legitimate debate about whether you can support a state like that and still have progressive” values. The boundary is contested inside the community it is drawn to protect.

items.event: J50 Declaration: fifty-nine Jewish organisations across forty countries declare anti-Zionism antisemitic
items.note: Issued in Jerusalem on the eve of Rosh Hashanah 5787 by seven global and regional bodies and fifty-two national and community bodies, reaffirming the IHRA working definition without reproducing either of its two limiting clauses. Two signatories, the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, are subject to the judgment delivered five weeks earlier.

items.event: NAZA wins the Special Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival
